specPoints.text: know that many reactions are readily reversible and that they can reach a state of dynamic equilibrium in which: i the rate of the forward reaction is equal to the rate of the backward reaction ii the concentrations of the reactants and the products remain constant

primer.text: Some reactions run both ways at once, and the two opposing half arrows say so. This note reaches dynamic equilibrium: forward and backward rates tied, concentrations constant yet unequal, and the whole balancing act demanding a closed system whenever gases would otherwise slip away.

lessons.title: Reversible reactions and the two-way arrow
lessons.opening: Some reactions refuse to finish: the products themselves re-form the reactants. The two half-arrows of the reversible equation announce a chemistry that runs in both directions at once, the seedbed of every equilibrium idea.
keyPoints: Reactions going to completion stop when reactants are fully used up.
Reversible reactions run backward too: their products rebuild the original reactants.
The reversible arrow (two opposing half arrows) marks a reaction running both ways.
Both the forward and the backward reaction occur simultaneously once products appear.

low.restatement: Completion reactions empty the reactant jar; reversible reactions keep refilling it from the products, so both directions run in the same vessel.
low.analogy: A leaky bucket that also refills from its own overflow: the water level settles somewhere in between, never empty, never full.
low.examPointer: Always use the equilibrium half-arrows in equations once reversibility is claimed - a single arrow wrongly implies completion.

medium.restatement: Reversibility means the product molecules retain the ability to regenerate reactants; the forward rate starts high and falls, the backward rate starts at zero and rises, and they converge at equilibrium.
medium.analogy: Two escalators running in opposite directions with shifting passenger flows that eventually balance.
medium.examPointer: Label forward and backward rates on sketches; equilibrium is where they cross, not where the concentrations are equal.

check.stem: In a reversible reaction, the products

options.text: Can react with each other to reform the original reactants
options.explanation: The backward reaction regenerates reactants from products.

options.text: Accumulate until the reactants are gone forever
options.explanation: That describes a completion reaction.

options.text: Are always solids
options.explanation: Reversibility is independent of physical state.

options.text: Stop forming once equilibrium is reached
options.explanation: Both directions continue; only the rates equalise.

check.stem: The symbol marking a reversible reaction is

options.text: Two opposing half arrows
options.explanation: The paired arrows declare simultaneous forward and backward chemistry.

options.text: A single forward arrow
options.explanation: That denotes completion.

options.text: A double equals sign
options.explanation: That is not reaction notation.

options.text: A curved arrow showing electron movement
options.explanation: Curly arrows belong to mechanisms.

check.stem: A reaction that goes to completion stops when

options.text: All of the reactants are used up
options.explanation: Depletion of reactants halts a completion reaction.

options.text: The products begin to reform reactants
options.explanation: Reforming is the reversible case.

options.text: Half the reactants remain
options.explanation: Nothing in completion chemistry stops the reaction midway.

options.text: The rate becomes constant and non-zero
options.explanation: Completion reactions end at rate zero.

check.stem: In a reversible reaction, the backward reaction begins

options.text: As soon as product molecules exist
options.explanation: Any product can immediately react to reform reactants.

options.text: Only after all reactants are consumed
options.explanation: Both directions run simultaneously once products appear.

options.text: Only when a catalyst is added
options.explanation: Catalysts are irrelevant to reversibility.

options.text: Never in a closed flask
options.explanation: Closed systems are exactly where both directions proceed.

check.stem: Which statement about the forward and backward rates before equilibrium is correct?

options.text: The forward rate starts high and falls; the backward starts at zero and rises
options.explanation: Their convergence defines the equilibrium state.

options.text: Both start at zero
options.explanation: The forward reaction begins immediately at full reactant availability.

options.text: Both stay constant until equilibrium
options.explanation: Rates evolve as compositions shift.

options.text: The backward rate always exceeds the forward
options.explanation: At equilibrium they are equal; before it, forward dominates.

check.stem: State what the two half arrows in a reaction equation represent.
check.modelAnswer: The simultaneous forward reaction (reactants to products) and backward reaction (products to reactants).

check.stem: Distinguish a completion reaction from a reversible reaction.
check.modelAnswer: A completion reaction stops when reactants are exhausted; a reversible reaction has products that reform the reactants, so both directions continue.

check.stem: Explain why the forward rate of a reversible reaction falls with time.
check.modelAnswer: Reactant concentration drops as the forward reaction proceeds, so collisions between reactant particles become less frequent and the forward rate declines.

check.stem: Ammonia synthesis N2 + 3H2 <=> 2NH3 runs in a sealed vessel. Explain why some nitrogen remains however long the reaction runs.
check.modelAnswer: The backward reaction converts ammonia back into nitrogen and hydrogen; as ammonia accumulates the backward rate rises until it matches the forward rate, so nitrogen never fully disappears.

lessons.title: Dynamic equilibrium and the closed system
lessons.opening: Equilibrium is motion in balance: forward and backward rates equal, concentrations constant - but not equal to each other. And the balance needs walls: gases reach equilibrium only in closed systems, though solution reactions manage even in open flasks.
keyPoints: In dynamic equilibrium the forward and backward rates are equal in a closed system, and concentrations stay constant.
Equilibrium concentrations are constant, not equal - the common misconception the examiners love.
A closed system loses neither reactants nor products; an open system can lose matter and energy.
Gas equilibria need closed vessels; solution reactions in open flasks lose negligible material by evaporation.

low.restatement: At equilibrium both reactions still run at identical rates, freezing the composition in place; the freezing requires a closed vessel when gases would otherwise escape.
low.analogy: A conveyer belt feeding a leak-proof warehouse at exactly the rate stock leaves the shelves: levels steady, movement never ceasing.
low.examPointer: Write 'constant, not equal' when describing equilibrium concentrations - the exact misconception examiners set as distractors.

medium.restatement: Dynamic equilibrium is a kinetic steady state: two opposing rates cancel in effect. Closure matters because escaping matter cannot be replaced by the backward reaction; open flasks still work for solutions where evaporation is negligible.
medium.analogy: Two identical pumps pushing water around a sealed loop keep levels fixed; unplug the loop and the levels drift.
medium.examPointer: Quote the hydrogen iodide example (2HI <=> H2 + I2) when asked to illustrate a dynamic equilibrium.

check.stem: At dynamic equilibrium, the concentrations of reactants and products are

options.text: Constant, but not necessarily equal
options.explanation: Rates equalise; concentrations freeze wherever the balance sits.

options.text: Always equal to each other
options.explanation: Equality of concentration is the classic misconception.

options.text: Both still changing steadily
options.explanation: Constant composition is the defining feature.

options.text: Both zero
options.explanation: Equilibrium mixtures contain both reactants and products.

check.stem: The word dynamic in dynamic equilibrium signals that

options.text: Both reactions continue at equal rates
options.explanation: Molecules keep reacting both ways; the composition merely stops changing.

options.text: The reaction has completely stopped
options.explanation: That is static, the opposite of the intended meaning.

options.text: The mixture is being heated
options.explanation: No temperature claim is packed into the word.

options.text: Products dominate the mixture
options.explanation: Position can favour either side.

check.stem: Why must gaseous equilibria be set up in closed systems?

options.text: Escaping gas would be unreplaced, driving the composition ever forward to completion
options.explanation: The backward reaction needs the products retained in the vessel.

options.text: Gases cannot react in open vessels
options.explanation: They react fine; the issue is loss of matter.

options.text: Closed systems lower the activation energy
options.explanation: Closure has nothing to do with Ea.

options.text: Pressure changes would poison the catalyst
options.explanation: No catalyst is involved in the definition.

check.stem: A solution reaction can approach equilibrium in an open flask because

options.text: Negligible material is lost by evaporation
options.explanation: What stays in the vessel participates in both directions.

options.text: Liquids cannot evaporate at all
options.explanation: They evaporate slowly; negligible is the operative word.

options.text: Open flasks are sealed at the top
options.explanation: By definition they are not.

options.text: Solutions bypass equilibrium entirely
options.explanation: Solution reactions reach equilibrium readily.

check.stem: In the hydrogen iodide equilibrium shown in the diagram, at equilibrium

options.text: HI decomposes to H2 and I2 at exactly the rate they recombine to HI
options.explanation: The snapshot shows both directions running in balance.

options.text: HI has entirely decomposed
options.explanation: Equilibrium mixtures retain reactant HI.

options.text: Only H2 and I2 are present
options.explanation: Both sides of the equation persist.

options.text: All concentrations are zero
options.explanation: Composition is constant and non-zero.

check.modelAnswer: A system from which none of the reactants or products can escape the reaction mixture.

check.stem: State the two defining features of dynamic equilibrium.
check.modelAnswer: Equal forward and backward rates in a closed system, and constant concentrations of reactants and products.

check.stem: Explain why equilibrium concentrations differ between a mixture approached from reactants and one approached from products.
check.modelAnswer: Position depends on composition and conditions; approaching from either side converges to the same equilibrium composition only when the overall starting atom counts match, otherwise different constants mixtures result.

check.stem: Calcium carbonate decomposes in a closed crucible and in an open dish. Predict and explain the different outcomes.
check.modelAnswer: Closed: CO2 is retained, so CaCO3 <=> CaO + CO2 establishes equilibrium with all three present. Open: CO2 escapes, the backward reaction cannot run, and decomposition proceeds to completion.

glossary.definition: A reaction whose products rebuild the original reactants, written with two opposing half arrows.
The state in a closed system where forward and backward rates are equal and concentrations remain constant.
A setup from which no reactant or product can escape the reaction mixture.
A setup losing matter or energy to the surroundings, which prevents gas equilibria.
